narrative:
The model estimates a 47% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three main factors shaped this outlook. First, your total years of experience across all jobs stands out as the strongest influence, but in the direction of staying rather than leaving. Most employees the model expects to remain have similarly modest overall experience, so the system sees your background as fairly typical for loyal staff.

The second most important factor works against you: you have received other job offers while at the company. This is relatively uncommon—only about 23% of employees predicted to stay reported receiving outside opportunities. The model interprets this as a clear sign that you have attractive alternatives, increasing the likelihood you might depart.

Third, your employment in the “other” sector also nudged the prediction upward. While this sector represents 22% of employees expected to stay, the model has learned that people in these varied roles tend to show slightly higher turnover than those in medical or education fields.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and sector slightly outweighs the stabilizing effect of your experience level, tipping the prediction toward leaving. The organization should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether stronger retention measures, such as clearer advancement paths, could address the external pull you are feeling.
